justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption across all three horizons, starting near the current price level and gradually stepping higher. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 290 is essentially anchored to the prevailing market price, with very little expected directional movement given the absence of a clear near-term catalyst. The one-week estimate of 292 incorporates a slight positive drift consistent with the long-run tendency of equity indices to trend upward, while the one-month estimate of 296 extends that drift further, implying no major regime change over the period. In each case, I treated recent price history and baseline equity market momentum as the primary drivers, without assuming any specific fundamental news event.

The confidence interval widths expand as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty in financial prices. At one day, realized volatility in large equity instruments tends to be modest in calm regimes, so the 279–301 range captures roughly the typical daily swing. By one week, a wider range of macro data releases, Fed communications, and global risk events can accumulate, pushing the interval to 271–313. At one month, the interval widens further to 252–340, capturing a realistic range of outcomes including mild bull or bear scenarios driven by earnings cycles, inflation data, or geopolitical developments.

There are several risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in risk sentiment — triggered by a credit event, an unexpected central bank pivot toward tightness, or an escalation in geopolitical conflict — could drive prices below 252 over the monthly horizon. Liquidity crunches or flash crash dynamics could even briefly breach the one-day interval. On the upside, a positive surprise on inflation or a dovish policy signal could fuel a momentum-driven rally that exceeds 340. My intervals are calibrated around a roughly normal return distribution, which means fat-tail events — which occur more frequently than a Gaussian model implies — are not fully captured at the stated confidence level.
